newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian investment sentiment improving - survey.
newsitem.headline: Australian investment sentiment improving - survey.

text.p: Australian investment sentiment has rebounded since February and the May 23 rate cut should help sentiment further, an IOOF/ASSIRT survey has found.
The survey's investment sentiment index rose to 37 points in June from 29 points in February.
The survey covered 2,013 adult Australians and was conducted prior to the last easing in monetary policy.
"The rebound in investment sentiment is a sign that recent interest rate cuts are starting to have a positive effect," IOOF senior economist Frank Uhlenbruch said in a statement.

In February, despite there having been three rate cuts since July 1996, investment sentiment had fallen, so the rebound seen since then was encouraging, and the latest cut may still have some impact, he said.

Survey participants were asked whether it was a good or bad time to be investing in six sectors -- investment property, own home, Australian shares, cash, Australian fixed interest, and superannuation.
The strongest rises were in "own home", where the sentiment index rose to 66 points from 40 in February, and "investment property", where the index rose to 54 points from 49 points.
"This bodes well for a recovery in the housing sector over 1997/98 (July/June)," Uhlenbruch said.
Two of the sentiment indexes, cash and fixed interest, were introduced for the June survey.
The cash index, which measures sentiment towards investments such as bank deposits and cash management trusts, recorded a reading of zero, while fixed interest sentiment was at seven points.
"The current bull run in the share market will be contributing to the neutral reading for the cash sector," ASSIRT manager of market research Kathleen Tepana said.
At face value, the reults suggested that further high levels of funds flow into cash may cease while the share market was powering ahead, she said.
Against this, some investors thought it was a good time to invest in cash, which may be due to perceptions that equities are overvalued and cash is a temporary safe haven, Tepana said.
The fixed interest reading reflected a view that the interest rate cycle had bottomed, or was close to it.
"Whilst real running yields are attractive, there is not much reward at present for investors to invest in longer dated bonds if yields are expected to rise from here," Tepana said.
The superannuation index remained steady, rising one point to 29 points in June, while the share sentiment index remained unchanged at 31 points.
Tepana said current superannuation investors were particularly positve about superannuation, most probably due to the healthy returns they are achieving as a resutl of share market exposure.
The share sentiment index showed share investors were more positive about shares compared to all investors and non-investors, a result not surprising given the share market's recent performance.
"This suggests that share investors are satisfied with the current performance of shares and most do not intend switching to alternative investments at this stage," Tepana said.
"Clearly share investors are not seeing significant risk of a market correction," she said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
